Duration::mod¶

Back to Duration API Reference

Signature¶

Duration Duration::mod(std::int64_t k) const;

What It Does¶

Computes the remainder of a Duration’s underlying nanosecond count after division by k — unlike mul/div/floordiv, whose k is a plain unit-agnostic count, mod’s k is always a raw nanosecond divisor. Computing “remainder after dividing by 3 days” means passing 3 * 86'400 * 1'000'000'000LL, not 3 — passing the bare integer 3 would compute “nanoseconds mod 3 nanoseconds,” not “mod 3 days.”

Parameters¶

k (std::int64_t)

A raw nanosecond divisor — not a plain count the way mul/div/floordiv’s k is. Convert explicitly (see Example 1).

Returns¶

Duration A new duration holding the elementwise remainder.

Examples¶

Example 1. mod against a three-day divisor, over a Duration array.

auto ranged = pluss::duration::range(
    pluss::duration::days(0), pluss::duration::days(10), pluss::duration::days(2));
constexpr std::int64_t kThreeDaysNanos = 3LL * 86'400 * 1'000'000'000LL;
std::cout << pluss::duration::print(ranged.mod(kThreeDaysNanos));

Output¶

Duration(shape=[6], dim=1, numel=6)
[ 0 days 00:00:00.000000000, 2 days 00:00:00.000000000, 1 days 00:00:00.000000000, 0 days 00:00:00.000000000, 2 days 00:00:00.000000000, 1 days 00:00:00.000000000 ]

[0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10] days each mod 3 days, elementwise: 0, 2, 1, 0, 2, 1. k had to be 3 * 86'400 * 1'000'000'000 (three days’ worth of nanoseconds), not the bare integer 3 — passing 3 would compute “days mod 3 nanoseconds,” not “days mod 3 days.”

Notes¶

  • mod’s divisor is always raw nanoseconds, regardless of what unit you’re conceptually thinking in — this is the one arithmetic method here that doesn’t take a plain, unit-agnostic count.

  • There is no Duration.mod(Duration) overload — see mul’s notes for why elapsed-time-times-elapsed-time isn’t representable here.

See Also¶

  • floordiv: the quotient complementary to this remainder.

  • div: exact division by a plain count.
